facts.text: Pasibutbut, often called the prayer for a good millet harvest, is a song of the Bunun, one of Taiwan's indigenous peoples.
Each year in November or December, when the Bunun hold their millet-sowing ceremony, the men of a community stand in a circle and sing the song to pray for a good millet crop.
The Bunun believe that the better the singing, the happier the god in the sky, and the more the millet will bear.
In the version sung at Mingde village, eight adult men sing in four voice parts (three, one, two and two singers), using only vowel sounds with no words.
The singers keep their arms linked around one another in a circle and move slowly counterclockwise; when the song ends they stop and raise their heads toward the sky.
One singer starts the first note; the other parts enter one by one below it, and the top part keeps pushing the pitch upward by steps smaller than a half step, so the whole chord slowly climbs.
The song closes on a wide, full chord that the Bunun call bisosilin; it is said to be the sound their sky god likes best.
Only two of the five Bunun groups, the Takbanuaz and the Isbukun, traditionally sing pasibutbut; the three more northern groups did not.
In 1943 the Japanese musicologist Kurosawa Takatomo recorded the song in what is now Kanding Village, Haiduan Township, Taitung, with help from Japanese police and a young Bunun man.
In 1952 Kurosawa sent the recording to the International Folk Music Council, a body linked to UNESCO.
Well-known Western music scholars, including Curt Sachs, Jaap Kunst and Andre Schaeffner, took notice of the recording.

A widely repeated account says scholars were amazed that an old mountain community sang such complex harmony, and that the song upset the Western theory that music grew from single tones to two tones and only later to harmony.
The name eight-part harmony is popular rather than exact: the song is built on four voice parts.
Between 1992 and 1995, ethnomusicologist Wu Rung-shun analyzed 25 recordings of pasibutbut with a sound spectrograph in Paris.

Wu found that a throaty vowel e and a special way of using the throat make strong overtones, extra higher tones above the sung notes, reaching as high as the 30th overtone; listeners therefore hear many more parts than are being sung.
Wu notes that many villages have added singers to try to create the eight-part effect, but more voices alone cannot produce it without the right vowels and throat technique.
Wu concludes that the Bunun name for the effect is not a myth: the people's ears picked up a real sound that outsiders had missed.
In October 2015, Hualien County registered Bunun pasibutbut music as a traditional performing art under its cultural heritage rules.
Once bound up with ritual and taboos, pasibutbut is now also performed on modern stages.
